{{short description|Directed path algebra}}

In mathematics, a '''Leavitt path algebra''' is an [[Algebra over a field|algebra]] constructed from a directed graph.  Leavitt path algebras generalize [[Leavitt algebra]]s and may be considered as algebraic analogues of [[graph C*-algebras]].

==History==
Leavitt path algebras were simultaneously introduced in 2005 by [[Gene Abrams]] and Gonzalo Aranda Pino<ref>Abrams, Gene; Aranda Pino, Gonzalo; The Leavitt path algebra 
of a graph. ''J. Algebra'' 293 (2005), no. 2, 319–334.</ref> as well as by Pere Ara, María Moreno, and Enrique Pardo,<ref>Pere Ara, María A. Moreno, and Enrique Pardo. Nonstable K-theory for 
graph algebras. ''Algebr. Represent. Theory'' 10(2):157–178, 2007.</ref> with neither of the two groups aware of the other's work.<ref>Sec. 1.7 of ''Leavitt Path Algebras'', Springer, London, 2017. {{citation|url=https://academics.uccs.edu/gabrams/documents/versionsenttoSpringer4April2017.pdf|title=Online Copy}}</ref>  Leavitt path algebras have been investigated by dozens of mathematicians since their introduction, and in 2020 Leavitt path algebras were added to the [[Mathematics Subject Classification]] with code 16S88 under the general discipline of Associative Rings and Algebras.<ref>{{citation|url=https://mathscinet.ams.org/msnhtml/msc2020.pdf|title=2020 Mathematics Subject Classification}}</ref>

The basic reference is the book ''Leavitt Path Algebras''.<ref name="lpa"> {{citation|url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-1-4471-7344-1 |author=Gene Abrams, Pere Ara, Mercedes Siles Molina  |title=Leavitt Path Algebras|publisher=Springer, London|series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics |year=2017 |volume=2191 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4471-7344-1 |isbn=978-1-4471-7343-4 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

==Graph terminology==
The theory of Leavitt path algebras uses terminology for graphs similar to that of C*-algebraists, which differs slightly from that used by graph theorists.  The term '''graph''' is typically taken to mean a [[directed graph]] <math>E=(E^0, E^1, r, s)</math> consisting of a [[countable set]] of vertices <math>E^0</math>, a countable set of edges <math>E^1</math>, and maps <math>r, s : E^1 \rightarrow E^0</math> identifying the range and source of each edge, respectively.  A vertex <math>v \in E^0</math> is called a '''sink''' when <math>s^{-1}(v) = \emptyset</math>; i.e., there are no edges in <math>E</math> with source <math>v</math>.  A vertex <math>v \in E^0</math> is called an '''infinite emitter''' when <math>s^{-1}(v)</math> is infinite; i.e., there are infinitely many edges in <math>E</math> with source <math>v</math>.  A vertex is called a '''singular vertex''' if it is either a sink or an infinite emitter, and a vertex is called a '''regular vertex''' if it is not a singular vertex.  Note that a vertex <math>v</math> is regular [[if and only if]] the number of edges in <math>E</math> with source <math>v</math> is finite and nonzero.  A graph is called '''row-finite''' if it has no infinite emitters; i.e., if every vertex is either a regular vertex or a sink.

A '''path''' is a finite sequence of edges <math>e_1 e_2 \ldots e_n</math> with <math>r(e_i) = s(e_{i+1})</math> for all <math>1 \leq i \leq n-1</math>.  An '''infinite path''' is a countably infinite sequence of edges <math>e_1 e_2 \ldots </math> with <math>r(e_i) = s(e_{i+1})</math> for all <math>i \in \mathbb{N}</math>.    A '''cycle''' is a path <math>e_1 e_2 \ldots e_n</math> with <math>r(e_n) = s(e_1)</math>, and an '''exit''' for a cycle <math>e_1 e_2 \ldots e_n</math> is an edge <math>f \in E^1</math> such that <math>s(f) = s(e_i)</math> and <math>f \neq e_i</math> for some <math>1 \leq i \leq n</math>.  A cycle <math>e_1 e_2 \ldots e_n</math> is called a '''simple cycle''' if <math>s(e_i) \neq s(e_1)</math> for all <math>2 \leq i \leq n</math>.

The following are two important graph conditions that arise in the study of Leavitt path algebras.

'''Condition (L):'''  Every cycle in the graph has an exit.

'''Condition (K):''' There is no vertex in the graph that is on exactly one simple cycle.  Equivalently, a graph satisfies Condition (K) if and only if each vertex in the graph is either on no cycles or on two or more simple cycles.

==The Cuntz–Krieger relations and the universal property==
Fix a field <math>K</math>.  A '''Cuntz–Krieger <math>E</math>-family''' is a collection <math>\{ s_e^*, s_e, p_v : e \in E^1, v \in E^0 \}</math> in a <math>K</math>-algebra such that the following three relations (called the '''Cuntz–Krieger relations''') are satisfied:

: (CK0) <math> p_v p_w = \begin{cases} p_v & \text{if } v=w \\ 0 &  \text{if } v\neq w \end{cases} \quad</math> for all <math>v, w \in E^0</math>,
: (CK1) <math> s_e^* s_f = \begin{cases} p_{r(e)} & \text{if } e=f \\ 0 &  \text{if } e\neq f \end{cases} \quad</math> for all <math>e, f \in E^1</math>,
: (CK2) <math>p_v = \sum_{s(e)=v} s_e s_e^*</math> whenever <math>v</math> is a regular vertex, and
: (CK3) <math>p_{s(e)} s_e = s_e</math> for all <math>e \in E^1</math>.

The Leavitt path algebra corresponding to <math>E</math>, denoted by <math>L_K(E)</math>, is defined to be the <math>K</math>-algebra generated by a Cuntz–Krieger <math>E</math>-family that is '''universal''' in the sense that whenever <math>\{ t_e, t_e^*, q_v : e \in E^1, v \in E^0 \}</math> is a Cuntz–Krieger <math>E</math>-family in a <math>K</math>-algebra <math>A</math> there exists a <math>K</math>-algebra homomorphism <math>\phi : L_K(E) \to A</math> with <math>\phi(s_e) = t_e</math> for all <math>e \in E^1</math>, <math>\phi(s_e^*) = t_e^*</math> for all <math>e \in E^1</math>, and <math>\phi(p_v)=q_v</math> for all <math>v \in E^0</math>.   

We define <math>p_v^* := p_v</math> for <math>v \in E^0</math>, and for a path <math>\alpha := e_1 \ldots e_n</math> we define <math>s_\alpha := s_{e_1} \ldots s_{e_n}</math> and <math>s_\alpha^* := s_{e_n}^* \ldots s_{e_1}^*</math>.  Using the Cuntz–Krieger relations, one can show that 

:<math>L_K(E) = \operatorname{span}_K \{ s_\alpha s_\beta^* : \alpha \text{ and } \beta \text{ are paths in } E \}.</math>

Thus a typical element of <math>L_K(E)</math> has the form <math>\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i s_{\alpha_i} s_{\beta_i}^*</math> for scalars <math>\lambda_1, \ldots,\lambda_n \in K</math> and paths <math>\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n, \beta_1, \ldots, \beta_n</math> in <math>E</math>.  If <math>K</math> is a field with an involution <math>\lambda \mapsto \overline{\lambda}</math> (e.g., when <math>K=\mathbb{C}</math>), then one can define a *-operation on <math>L_K(E)</math> by <math>\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i s_{\alpha_i} s_{\beta_i}^* \mapsto \sum_{i=1}^n \overline{\lambda_i} s_{\beta_i} s_{\alpha_i}^*</math> that makes <math>L_K(E)</math> into a *-algebra.

Moreover, one can show that for any graph <math>E</math>, the Leavitt path algebra <math>L_{\mathbb{C}}(E)</math> is isomorphic to a dense *-subalgebra of the graph C*-algebra <math>C^*(E)</math>.

==Correspondence between graph and algebraic properties==
As with graph C*-algebras, graph-theoretic properties of <math>E</math> correspond to algebraic properties of <math>L_K(E)</math>.  Interestingly, it is often the case that the graph properties of <math>E</math> that are equivalent to an algebraic property of <math>L_K(E)</math> are the same graph properties of <math>E</math> that are equivalent to corresponding C*-algebraic property of <math>C^*(E)</math>, and moreover, many of the properties for <math>L_K(E)</math> are independent of the field <math>K</math>.

The following table provides a short list of some of the more well-known equivalences.  The reader may wish to compare this table with the [[graph C*-algebra#Correspondence between graph and C*-algebraic properties|corresponding table for graph C*-algebras]].

 {| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;"
|-
! {{larger|Property of <math>E</math>}} !! {{larger|Property of <math>L_K(E)</math>}}
|-
| <math>E</math> is a finite, acylic graph. || <math>L_K(E)</math> is finite dimensional.
|-
| The vertex set <math>E^0</math> is finite. || <math>L_K(E)</math> is unital (i.e., <math>L_K(E)</math> contains a multiplicative identity).
|-
| <math>E</math> has no cycles. || <math>L_K(E)</math> is an ultramatrical <math>K</math>-algebra (i.e., a direct limit of finite-dimensional <math>K</math>-algebras).
|-
|  style="text-align:left;" | <math>E</math> satisfies the following three properties:
# Condition (L), 
# for each vertex <math>v</math> and each infinite path <math>\alpha</math> there exists a directed path from <math>v</math> to a vertex on <math>\alpha</math>, and 
#for each vertex <math>v</math> and each singular vertex <math>w</math> there exists a directed path from <math>v</math> to <math>w</math>
|| <math>L_K(E)</math> is simple.

# for each vertex <math>v</math> in <math>E</math> there is a path from <math>v</math> to a cycle. 
|| Every left ideal of <math>L_K(E)</math> contains an infinite idempotent.  <br>(When <math>L_K(E)</math> is simple this is equivalent to <math>L_K(E)</math> being a purely infinite ring.)
|}

==The grading==
For a path <math>\alpha := e_1 \ldots e_n</math> we let <math>|\alpha| := n</math> denote the length of <math>\alpha</math>.  For each integer <math>n \in \mathbb{Z}</math> we define <math>L_K(E)_n := \operatorname{span}_K \{ s_\alpha s_\beta^* : |\alpha|-|\beta| = n \}</math>.  One can show that this defines a [[graded ring|<math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-grading]] on the Leavitt path algebra <math>L_K(E)</math> and that <math>L_K(E) = \bigoplus_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} L_K(E)_n</math> with <math>L_K(E)_n</math> being the component of homogeneous elements of degree <math>n</math>. The grading depends on the choice of the generating Cuntz-Krieger <math>E</math>-family <math>\{ s_e, s_e^*, p_v : e \in E^1, v \in E^0 \}</math>.  The grading on the Leavitt path algebra <math>L_K(E)</math> is the algebraic analogue of [[graph C*-algebra#The gauge action|the gauge action on the graph C*-algebra <math>C*(E)</math>]], and it is a fundamental tool in analyzing the structure of <math>L_K(E)</math>.

==The uniqueness theorems==
There are two well-known uniqueness theorems for Leavitt path algebras: the graded uniqueness theorem and the Cuntz-Krieger uniqueness theorem.  These are analogous, respectively, to [[graph C*-algebra#The uniqueness theorems|the gauge-invariant uniqueness theorem and Cuntz-Krieger uniqueness theorem for graph C*-algebras]].  Formal statements of the uniqueness theorems are as follows:

'''The ''Graded'' Uniqueness Theorem:'''  Fix a field <math>K</math>.  Let <math>E</math> be a graph, and let <math>L_K(E)</math> be the associated Leavitt path algebra.  If <math>A</math> is a ''graded'' <math>K</math>-algebra and <math>\phi : L_K(E) \to A</math> is a graded algebra homomorphism with <math>\phi(p_v) \neq 0</math> for all <math>v \in E^0</math>, then <math>\phi</math> is injective.

'''The Cuntz-Krieger Uniqueness Theorem:'''   Fix a field <math>K</math>.  Let <math>E</math> be a graph satisfying Condition (L), and let <math>L_K(E)</math> be the associated Leavitt path algebra.  If <math>A</math> is a <math>K</math>-algebra and <math>\phi : L_K(E) \to A</math> is an algebra homomorphism with <math>\phi(p_v) \neq 0</math> for all <math>v \in E^0</math>, then <math>\phi</math> is injective.

==Ideal structure==
We use the term ideal to mean "two-sided ideal" in our Leavitt path algebras.  The ideal structure of <math>L_K(E)</math> can be determined from <math>E</math>.  A subset of vertices <math>H \subseteq E^0</math> is called '''hereditary''' if for all <math>e \in E^1</math>, <math>s(e) \in H</math> implies <math>r(e) \in H</math>.  A hereditary subset <math>H</math> is called '''saturated''' if whenever <math>v</math> is a regular vertex with <math>r(s^{-1}(v)) \subseteq H</math>, then <math>v \in H</math>.  The saturated hereditary subsets of <math>E</math> are partially ordered by inclusion, and they form a lattice with meet <math>H_1 \wedge H_2 := H_1 \cap H_2</math> and join <math>H_1 \vee H_2</math> defined to be the smallest saturated hereditary subset containing <math>H_1 \cup H_2</math>.

If <math>H</math> is a saturated hereditary subset, <math>I_H</math> is defined to be two-sided ideal in <math>L_K(E)</math> generated by <math>\{ p_v : v \in H \}</math>.  A two-sided ideal <math>I</math> of <math>L_K(E)</math> is called a '''graded ideal''' if the <math>I</math> has a <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-grading <math>I = \bigoplus_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} I_n</math> and <math>I_n = L_K(E)_n \cap I</math> for all <math>n \in \mathbb{Z}</math>.  The graded ideals are partially ordered by inclusion and form a lattice with meet <math>I_1 \wedge I_2 := I_1 \cap I_2</math> and joint <math>I_1 \vee I_2</math> defined to be the ideal generated by <math>I_1 \cup I_2</math>.  For any saturated hereditary subset <math>H</math>, the ideal <math>I_H</math> is graded.

The following theorem describes how graded ideals of <math>L_K(E)</math> correspond to saturated hereditary subsets of <math>E</math>.

'''Theorem:'''  Fix a field <math>K</math>, and let <math>E</math> be a row-finite graph.  Then the following hold:
# The function <math>H \mapsto I_H</math> is a lattice isomorphism from the lattice of saturated hereditary subsets of <math>E</math> onto the lattice of graded ideals of <math>L_K(E)</math> with inverse given by <math>I \mapsto \{ v \in E^0 : p_v \in I \}</math>.  
# For any saturated hereditary subset <math>H</math>, the quotient <math>L_K(E)/I_H</math> is <math>*</math>-isomorphic to <math>L_K(E \setminus H)</math>, where <math>E \setminus H</math> is the subgraph of <math>E</math> with vertex set <math>(E \setminus H)^0 := E^0 \setminus H</math> and edge set <math>(E \setminus H)^1 := E^1 \setminus r^{-1}(H)</math>.
# For any saturated hereditary subset <math>H</math>, the ideal <math>I_H</math> is [[Morita equivalence|Morita equivalent]] to <math>L_K(E_H)</math>, where <math>E_H</math> is the subgraph of <math>E</math> with vertex set <math>E_H^0 := H</math> and edge set <math>E_H^1 := s^{-1}(H)</math>.
# If <math>E</math> satisfies Condition (K), then every ideal of <math>L_K(E)</math> is graded, and the ideals of <math>L_K(E)</math> are in one-to-one correspondence with the saturated hereditary subsets of <math>E</math>.
